seoTitle: How to Add Nifty Options in TradingView the Right Way
metaDescription: Find the exact Nifty options contract on TradingView: why a plain search returns the spot index instead, how to filter to Options, and how real-time NSE data access works.
intro: Typing "Nifty" into TradingView's search bar gets you the spot index or a futures contract almost every time, not the specific options contract you meant to chart. Options symbols are named with a strict code bundling the expiry date, contract type, and strike price together, and unless you filter for it directly, it's easy to end up analyzing the wrong instrument entirely. This guide covers how to search properly, filter down to Options, and read the strike-and-expiry list so you load the exact CE or PE contract you meant to trade.

steps.heading: Open the symbol search
steps.body: From any TradingView chart or the homepage, click the search bar at the top, or press Ctrl+K on Windows and Cmd+K on Mac, to open the symbol search panel. It's the same search used for stocks, futures, and forex, which is exactly why a plain "Nifty" query returns a mix of everything instead of the option contract you're after.

steps.heading: See what a plain Nifty search returns
steps.body: Typing the symbol brings back a mixed list: the Nifty 50 spot index, Bank Nifty, Dow Jones, and other unrelated tickers sorted by relevance instead of by contract type. An options-style entry can already be buried in there, like NIFTY260330P9000, which decodes as Nifty 50, expiring 30 March 2026, a Put, at strike 9000. Scrolling through a mixed list to find the right one isn't reliable, which is why filtering matters.

image.caption: A plain Nifty search returning a mix of instruments, the spot index, unrelated global tickers, and one options contract buried in the middle of the list.

steps.heading: A strike number in the query doesn't filter it either
steps.body: Searching something like "nifty 18000" without narrowing the instrument type still returns index and futures entries: Nifty 50 Index, Nifty Bank Index, GIFT Nifty 50 Index Futures. None of those is the options contract the number implies. The strike price you typed doesn't filter anything on its own, so it's easy to end up charting a futures contract while thinking you selected an option.

image.caption: The same kind of search without the Options filter applied, surfacing the spot index and futures contracts instead of the strike-specific option you're looking for.

steps.heading: Filter to Options
steps.body:
Above the results list, TradingView shows category tabs: All, Stocks, Funds, Futures, Forex, Crypto, Indices, Bonds, Economy, and Options. Click Options and the list changes to rows like NIFTY260217C26000 and NIFTY260217P26000, each formatted as symbol, expiry date, contract type, and strike. Add the exchange prefix "NSE:" to the same search to keep the list to NSE contracts specifically; TradingView's own help pages give this as the standard route to Indian options.

If you already know the exact contract you want, you can skip the scrolling: type the ticker straight into the search box, for example NIFTY260217C26000, and press Enter. TradingView opens it directly.

image.caption: The Options tab selected, listing CALL and PUT contracts for the same strike and a run of weekly expiry dates, this is where you pick the exact contract to chart.

steps.heading: Tell CE and PE apart, then load the chart
steps.body: The letter right after the expiry date in the symbol is the giveaway: C means Call (CE), P means Put (PE). NIFTY260217C19600 is a call at strike 19600 expiring 17 February 2026; the P version at the same strike and date is the matching put. Click the contract you want and TradingView shows it as the active symbol at the top of the panel, with a preview chart and a Full chart button to open it in the main workspace. Confirm you've clicked the right letter first. A call and a put at the identical strike and expiry behave very differently, and it's an easy click to get backwards in a long scrolling list.

image.caption: The selected option contract loaded as the active symbol, with a preview chart and a Full chart button to open it as your main chart.

steps.heading: Read the chart with options behaviour in mind
steps.body: Option charts move differently from the underlying index because price direction, time decay, and changing volatility are all baked in together, especially as expiry nears. Expect thinner volume and choppier candles than on the Nifty spot chart, particularly on strikes further from the current price. A contract's price history resets each time you roll to a new expiry too. There's no continuous multi-month chart the way there is for the underlying index.

costNote: Nifty options run on NSE data. TradingView's own documentation says non-professional users get real-time NSE futures and options data by default, at no extra cost, while accounts flagged as professional see delayed data unless they've signed the exchange's real-time data agreement. BSE options work differently: delayed by default for everyone, with a paid data package needed for real-time access. If a Nifty options chart looks like it's lagging the live market, that's the first thing to check on your account.

faq.question: Can I type the exact contract symbol instead of scrolling through the Options tab?
faq.answer: Yes. Typing a constructed ticker such as NIFTY260217C26000 into symbol search and pressing Enter opens that contract directly, per TradingView's own help documentation.

faq.question: How do I tell a call from a put in the symbol name?
faq.answer: Look at the letter right after the expiry date: C means Call, P means Put. NIFTY260217C19600 is a call; NIFTY260217P19600 is the matching put at the same strike and expiry.

faq.question: Why does my Nifty options data look delayed?
faq.answer: It depends on your account status. Non-professional TradingView users get real-time NSE options data by default; accounts flagged as professional see delayed data unless they've signed NSE's real-time data agreement.

faq.question: What's the difference between Nifty spot and Nifty options?
faq.answer: The spot index (NIFTY) reflects the live value of the underlying basket of stocks. Options are separate derivative contracts tied to that index, each with its own strike, expiry, and pricing, shown in results like NIFTY260217C19600.

faq.question: Do Nifty options expire, and does that affect the chart?
faq.answer: Yes. Each contract has a fixed expiry baked into its symbol, and its chart history only exists up to that date. There's no rolling continuous options chart the way there is for the spot index.

faq.question: Can I add a Nifty option to my watchlist?
faq.answer: Yes, once you've filtered to Options and found the specific contract through symbol search, you can add it to your watchlist the same way as any other symbol.
